title: Ask about the writer's structural choices
statement: Ask why a writer structured a text as they did, not how many paragraphs or headings it has, since the state reading test rewards explaining the writer's choices.
example: A learner who says a text's structure is that it has four paragraphs has counted its parts, not explained the writer's choices.
detail: In a build meeting on 8 October 2026, one participant said the state reading test asks learners not only to recognise a text's structure but to talk about the writer's choices, and that some questions in another reading course only asked them to spot features, such as how many headings an article has, which that test does not reward (`g9/sources/meeting-notes/Incept Service CoE Catchup - 2026_10_08 10_30 CEST - Notes by Gemini.md`, lines 366-370). The same participant said learners have a poor sense of why a writer has structured something and tend to think structure simply means how many paragraphs a text has (line 374). The transcript is machine-made, and its 'STAR' is the state test.
against: It is one person's account in a meeting, not a measured result.
